Vignette: Marta, Age 79

Marta was nineteen years old when the soldiers came through her village. It was the tail end of a brutal occupation, and what happened over those three days in the spring of 1964 — the ransacking of homes, the shooting of her neighbor in the street, and the night she spent hidden beneath the floorboards of her family's workshop while men moved through the rooms above her — left something permanently altered in her. She did not speak of it for decades. She married, raised three children, buried her husband six years ago, and for most of her adult life managed to keep the memories at a distance through the simple insistence of living. She built a small tailoring business from nothing, and the work — the measuring, the cutting, the long hours at the machine — gave her hands something to do and her mind somewhere to go that was not 1964.

Now, at seventy-nine, the distance is gone. Marta sits in the therapy room with her hands folded in her lap, and she describes a world that has become frightening in ways she struggles to articulate. She sleeps no more than three or four hours a night. When she does sleep, she is back under the floorboards — the weight of the darkness pressing down, the sound of boots on wood directly above her face. She wakes with her heart hammering and lies rigid in the dark of her apartment until morning comes. She has stopped closing the bedroom curtains because she cannot tolerate the feeling of being enclosed, though she cannot always explain this to herself.

During the day, the intrusions arrive without warning. A car backfiring on the street below sends her flat against the wall of her workroom, breathless, certain for a moment that the soldiers have returned. The smell of cigarette smoke — so ordinary, so everywhere — can pull her back completely, because the men above the floorboards had been smoking. She loses minutes this way. She finds herself standing at her cutting table with no memory of having walked there, scissors in hand, her chest tight and her vision narrowed.

The tailoring work has become both refuge and torment. She still takes in alterations, still receives the elderly women from her building who bring her their good coats and their wedding anniversary dresses. The routine steadies her. Her hands know what to do with fabric in a way that feels older and more reliable than thought. But she works alone now, and she prefers it that way. She has quietly withdrawn from the small social world she once maintained — the weekly card game, the Sunday lunches with her daughter's family. Crowds make her vigilant in a way that exhausts her. She finds herself scanning exits, watching strangers' hands, sitting always with her back to the wall. Her daughter has noticed that her mother has become "difficult," and Marta knows this is true. She is irritable in ways she cannot control, and she carries a low, persistent shame about it.

What troubles Marta most, she says, is that she believed she had survived. For sixty years she believed that. She raised children, she made beautiful things with her hands, she mourned her husband and continued. She did not understand that the thing under the floorboards had simply been waiting. She wonders now whether the structure of her working life — the discipline of the craft, the appointments, the steady forward movement of a bolt of fabric through a machine — had been holding it at bay all along, and whether what changed was not her, but the quietness of old age. There is too much silence now. Too much time. And in the silence, the spring of 1964 is always just beneath the surface, as close and as heavy as a set of boots on a wooden floor.
